before.content_html:
A Bicameral Parliament

The UK Parliament is bicameral, meaning it has two chambers: the House of Commons and the House of Lords. This two-chamber design means legislation is debated and scrutinised in two places before it becomes law. Parliament meets at the Palace of Westminster in London. Its three core functions are making laws (the legislative function), scrutinising the work of the government (the accountability function) and representing citizens and debating matters of public concern.

The House of Commons

The House of Commons is the elected chamber. It has 650 Members of Parliament (MPs), each representing a constituency — a local area of the country. MPs are elected by the public using the First Past the Post system. Because the Commons is democratically elected, it is the more powerful of the two chambers. It can pass laws, approve government spending, debate policy and hold ministers to account through parliamentary questions, select committees and debates.

The Commons is chaired by the Speaker, who maintains order in debates, decides who may speak and is politically neutral — resigning from their party upon election to the post. The whips are party officials who manage MPs’ attendance and voting behaviour. Front bench MPs — ministers in government, shadow ministers in opposition — sit nearest the despatch boxes. Back bench MPs sit behind them and can scrutinise and challenge the front bench from within their own party or from opposition.

Key Fact

MPs scrutinise the government through: parliamentary questions (including Prime Minister’s Questions, held weekly when Parliament is sitting); select committees (groups of MPs who investigate specific policy areas and publish reports); and debates (formal discussions in the Chamber on legislation, government policy or matters of public concern). Select committees can call ministers and civil servants to give evidence.

The House of Lords

The House of Lords is the upper chamber. Unlike the Commons, it is not elected — its members are mostly appointed. Lords come from three groups: life peers (appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister for their lifetime); bishops (26 senior Church of England bishops, known as Lords Spiritual); and hereditary peers (a small remaining group of 92, whose title passes down through their family following the House of Lords Act 1999). The Lords scrutinise and can amend legislation passed by the Commons. They cannot permanently block Bills or legislation relating to finance (money Bills), but they can delay Bills by up to a year and return them to the Commons with proposed amendments.

The unelected nature of the Lords is the subject of ongoing debate. Supporters argue that many life peers bring independent expertise (in law, science, medicine, the arts) that improves the quality of scrutiny. Critics argue that an unelected chamber exercising legislative power is incompatible with democratic principles. Both viewpoints reflect genuine arguments in the continuing debate over Lords reform.

Black Rod is an official of the House of Lords. The most visible ceremonial role of Black Rod is during the State Opening of Parliament, when they walk to the House of Commons to summon MPs to hear the King’s Speech. By tradition, the door of the Commons is shut in Black Rod’s face — symbolising the Commons’ independence from the Crown — before being opened after three knocks.

The State Opening of Parliament is a ceremony in which the monarch delivers the King’s Speech (or Queen’s Speech), which sets out the government’s legislative programme for the coming year. The speech is written by the government, not the monarch, reflecting the convention that the monarch acts on the advice of ministers. The Speaker chairs the House of Commons, selected by MPs and expected to be politically impartial, calling MPs to speak and maintaining order.

Key Fact

The House of Commons is elected (650 MPs, one per constituency). The House of Lords is mostly appointed (life peers, bishops, some hereditary peers). The Commons is the more powerful chamber: it can pass any legislation; the Lords can delay Bills and propose amendments but cannot permanently block them. Finance Bills (relating to taxation and spending) cannot be delayed by the Lords under the Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949.

One viewpoint is that the Lords should be reformed to include an elected element. Supporters of this view argue that democratic legitimacy requires elected representatives at every level of the legislature; that appointed peers may not reflect the diversity of the population; and that the current system allows Prime Ministers too much patronage power in deciding who becomes a lord.

A contrasting viewpoint is that the appointed nature of the Lords is a feature rather than a flaw. Supporters argue that life peers with expertise in specific fields (such as medical science, law or education) improve the quality of legislative scrutiny. They also argue that a fully elected second chamber could rival the Commons and create constitutional deadlock, whereas the current Lords acts as a revising chamber rather than a competing power. This debate is ongoing and reflects genuine disagreement about democratic values.

The Role of the Opposition

The largest party not in government forms the opposition. Its leader becomes Leader of the Opposition and leads a ‘shadow cabinet’ — shadow ministers who scrutinise each government department. At Prime Minister’s Questions (PMQs), the Leader of the Opposition questions the Prime Minister directly, putting the government’s record under public scrutiny. The formal existence of an organised opposition is a key feature of UK parliamentary democracy — it ensures the government must defend its decisions in public.

Why Voting Systems Matter

The way votes are counted determines who governs. Different voting systems can produce very different outcomes from the same set of votes. The UK uses several voting systems for different elections: First Past the Post (FPTP) for Westminster general elections, and various forms of proportional representation for devolved elections and some local elections. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of each system is a key citizenship skill.

First Past the Post (FPTP)

Under FPTP, the UK is divided into parliamentary constituencies. Each constituency elects one MP. Voters mark a cross next to their preferred candidate. The candidate with the most votes wins — they do not need a majority of votes, just more than anyone else. Westminster general elections use this system for all 650 seats.

Key Fact

Under FPTP, each constituency elects one MP — the candidate with the most votes wins, regardless of whether they have a majority. This is called a plurality. Westminster general elections take place every five years under this system.

Strengths of FPTP

Supporters of FPTP highlight several advantages. First, it usually produces a clear result: one party typically wins enough seats to form a majority government with a strong mandate to govern. Strong majority governments can implement their manifesto commitments without being blocked by coalition partners. Second, each MP represents a specific constituency, creating a direct link between voters and their elected representative. Third, the system is simple to understand and quick to count: voters mark one cross, results are declared overnight.

Supporters also argue that FPTP produces stability: governments tend to last a full term rather than collapsing when coalition partners fall out. The 2010–2015 coalition, though stable by comparative standards, showed the complexity of coalition negotiation that more proportional systems often require.

Weaknesses of FPTP

Critics of FPTP point to several serious problems. First, the system can produce large majorities from a minority of votes: a party can win a landslide majority in Parliament while winning well under half of the votes cast nationally, because votes for losing candidates in each constituency contribute nothing to the final seat count. Second, many votes are effectively “wasted” — in safe seats, the outcome is predictable regardless of the local vote, reducing the incentive to vote. Third, smaller parties that attract votes spread evenly across constituencies may win very few seats even with significant national support, meaning proportionality is low.

A very common exam error is to list FPTP advantages and disadvantages on one side, and proportional representation advantages and disadvantages on the other side, without comparing the two against each other. Examiners want explicit comparison and a substantiated judgement — for example: “While FPTP produces stable majority governments more reliably than PR, it does so at the cost of proportionality, which means millions of voters are effectively unrepresented. On balance, the gain in stability may or may not outweigh this democratic deficit depending on the criteria used.” A side-by-side list without explicit comparison and a conclusion will not reach the top band.

Proportional Representation Systems

Several forms of proportional representation (PR) are used in UK elections. These systems aim to ensure that parties win seats in rough proportion to their share of the vote, giving smaller parties and minority views better representation.

The Additional Member System (AMS) is used for elections to the Scottish Parliament and the Welsh Senedd. Voters cast two votes: one for a constituency MP (using FPTP) and one for a regional party list. The regional seats are allocated to correct for the disproportionality of the constituency results, producing an overall result closer to the share of the vote. The Scottish Parliament was designed to make single-party majority government difficult, encouraging coalition or minority government.

The Single Transferable Vote (STV) is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections and Scottish local government elections. Voters rank candidates 1, 2, 3, and so on. Votes are transferred according to these preferences until all seats are filled. STV produces highly proportional results and gives voters more choice, but is complex to count and can produce results that are harder for voters to understand immediately.

Key Fact

The Additional Member System is used for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd elections. The Single Transferable Vote is used for Northern Ireland Assembly elections. Both produce more proportional outcomes than FPTP.

Strengths and Weaknesses of PR

Supporters of proportional systems argue that they better represent the range of views in society. Smaller parties can win seats, reducing “wasted votes” and encouraging more people to vote because their vote is more likely to count. Coalitions, which PR tends to produce, can also represent a broader range of voters’ priorities.

Critics argue that PR produces weak governments: coalition partners may disagree, making it harder to implement a clear programme, and voters may not know which parties will form a government after the election. The relationship between individual voters and a specific representative can also be weakened when large multi-member constituencies replace single-member ones. There is no consensus in the UK about which system is best: this remains a contested political question on which different parties hold different positions.

In 2011, a UK-wide referendum was held on whether to replace FPTP for Westminster elections with the Alternative Vote (AV) system, in which voters rank candidates in order of preference and the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated in successive rounds until one candidate has more than half the votes. The proposal was rejected: 67.9% voted to keep FPTP and 32.1% voted for AV. The result showed that, at that point, a majority of UK voters preferred to keep the existing system. Supporters of reform argued the question was poorly framed and that AV was not a fully proportional system in any case. The debate about electoral reform continues, with supporters of more proportional systems arguing the 2011 referendum settled only the question of AV, not the broader principle of proportional representation.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • First Past the Post is used for Westminster elections: the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins the seat, which tends to produce majority governments but can produce disproportionate results.
  • Proportional systems (AMS for Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd; STV for Northern Ireland Assembly) give smaller parties fairer representation but can lead to coalition governments and may weaken the voter-MP link.
  • Evaluating voting systems means comparing them explicitly — choosing between stability, proportionality, simplicity and voter-representative links — rather than just listing features of each.

before.content_html:
Why Government Operates at Different Levels

The UK is governed at several levels: the UK-wide Westminster Parliament, devolved administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and elected local councils across England and the other nations. Each level has different responsibilities, different budgets and different electoral systems. This multi-layered structure means that decisions about a school in Cardiff are made differently from decisions about a hospital in Glasgow or a road in Somerset. Understanding which level of government does what is a key citizenship skill.

Local Government

Local government is delivered by elected councils. Local councils provide a wide range of services: collecting rubbish, maintaining roads and parks, running planning permission processes, providing social care for the elderly and vulnerable, overseeing housing, managing libraries and leisure facilities, and supporting schools. Some of these services are statutory duties (the council must provide them by law); others are discretionary (the council can choose to provide them if it has the funds).

Councils are led by elected councillors, each representing a ward (a local area). Councillors debate local issues, set the council’s budget and hold the council’s executive to account. They are directly accountable to residents: if voters are unhappy with their councillor, they can vote them out at local elections, which in England are typically held every four years. Councils raise some of their own income through council tax paid by local residents; the majority of their funding comes as grants from central government, which means central government retains significant influence over what councils can afford to do.

Key Fact

Local councils provide services including waste collection, social care, planning, roads and parks. They are led by elected councillors who are accountable to residents at local elections. Funding comes from council tax and central government grants.

Devolution

Devolution is the process by which powers are transferred from the Westminster Parliament to elected bodies in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Devolution does not mean independence: Westminster remains sovereign and can in theory reclaim devolved powers, though this would be politically highly controversial. Devolution was introduced following referendums in Scotland and Wales in 1997, and after the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland in 1998.

The Scottish Parliament was established in 1999 and has wide devolved powers, including health, education, justice, housing and some taxation. The Senedd (Welsh Parliament, known as the National Assembly for Wales until 2020) has grown in power through successive devolution Acts, gaining legislative and limited tax-varying powers. The Northern Ireland Assembly operates under a power-sharing arrangement between unionist and nationalist parties, reflecting the region’s political history.

Many students confuse devolution with independence. Devolution transfers specific powers to a regional parliament while Westminster retains overall sovereignty. Defence, foreign affairs, immigration and most taxation remain reserved to Westminster for all devolved nations — the Scottish Parliament cannot declare war or set its own immigration rules. Independence, by contrast, would mean Scotland (for example) leaving the UK entirely, with full sovereignty over all matters. The question of Scottish independence is a separate and contested political debate; devolution is the current constitutional arrangement. Conflating the two will lose marks in an exam answer.

Reserved and Devolved Powers

Reserved powers are those that remain with Westminster. They include: defence and armed forces; foreign affairs and international treaties; immigration and nationality; most social security benefits; broadcasting regulation; and the overall framework of macroeconomic policy. Devolved powers vary between the three nations but typically include health, education, housing, environment, transport (within the nation) and some aspects of justice. The Scottish Parliament has some income tax and stamp duty powers.

Key Fact

Reserved powers (kept at Westminster) include defence, foreign affairs and immigration. Devolved powers (transferred to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) include health, education and housing.

English Votes for English Laws (EVEL)

A long-running constitutional debate concerns the “West Lothian Question”: should Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish MPs at Westminster be able to vote on legislation that only affects England, given that English MPs cannot vote on equivalent matters devolved to the Scottish Parliament or other assemblies? One answer is the principle of English Votes for English Laws (EVEL).

Supporters of EVEL argue that democratic fairness requires English-only legislation to be decided by English representatives, just as Scottish health policy is decided by the Scottish Parliament. Critics argue it creates a two-tier Parliament, complicating decision-making by requiring different MPs to vote on different parts of the same bill, and risks deepening divisions between the nations of the UK. The debate reflects the broader tension in an asymmetric devolution settlement — one in which Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have devolved parliaments but England has none, meaning English governance remains almost entirely at Westminster level.

The extent of devolution — and whether it should be extended, reduced or lead to full independence — is a genuinely contested political question in the UK. Supporters of further devolution argue that decisions made closer to communities better reflect local needs and that democratic engagement is higher when people have genuine power over their own services. They point to Scotland’s different approach to university tuition fees or free personal care as evidence that devolution enables tailored policy.

Critics of further devolution argue that it risks fragmenting the UK, creating inequalities of provision between nations and regions, and making the UK less able to act coherently on shared challenges such as economic policy or defence. Some argue that local and regional variation, while attractive in principle, creates postcode lotteries where citizens’ access to services depends on where they happen to live. This debate has no settled answer and reflects genuine competing values: local democracy versus national unity and coherence.

glossary_terms.definition: Elected bodies responsible for providing local services and making decisions for their area, funded partly by central government grants and partly by local council tax.
Elected representatives who sit on a local council, represent a ward and are accountable to local residents for council decisions.
The transfer of powers from a central government to regional or national legislatures, while the central Parliament retains overall sovereignty.
The elected parliament of Scotland, established in 1999 with devolved powers including health, education and justice, using the Additional Member System.
The devolved legislature for Northern Ireland, established under the Good Friday Agreement 1998, with power-sharing between unionist and nationalist parties.
Policy areas retained by the Westminster Parliament and not transferred to devolved administrations, including defence, foreign affairs, immigration and most macroeconomic policy.
Policy areas transferred to devolved legislatures in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, such as health, education and housing.
A constitutional arrangement under which only English MPs may vote on legislation that applies only to England, to address the imbalance created by asymmetric devolution.

before.content_html:
Who Has the Right to Vote?

The right to vote in elections is not universal across every type of election held in the United Kingdom. To vote in a UK general election you must be aged 18 or over, a British citizen, a qualifying Commonwealth citizen or a qualifying Irish citizen, and you must be registered on the electoral roll. Being on the electoral roll means providing your name and address to your local council so that you appear on the official list of voters for your constituency.

The voting age differs for Scottish Parliament and Senedd (Welsh Parliament) elections, where the age is 16. This difference has prompted a national debate about whether the voting age for UK general elections should also be lowered to 16.

Key Fact

The minimum voting age for a UK general election is 18. The minimum voting age for the Scottish Parliament and the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) is 16. These are different rules in different elections within the same country.

Who Cannot Vote?

Certain groups are excluded from voting in UK general elections. Members of the House of Lords cannot vote in general elections because they are already part of Parliament as unelected members. People convicted of a serious criminal offence who are currently serving a custodial sentence are also excluded from voting during their time in prison. Additionally, anyone who is not registered to vote cannot cast a ballot, regardless of age or nationality.

Who Can Stand for Election?

To stand as a candidate in a UK general election, you must be aged 18 or over and a British citizen or qualifying Commonwealth or Irish citizen. However, some people are disqualified from standing even if they meet the basic requirements. Members of the House of Lords cannot stand for the Commons as MPs because they already sit in Parliament. Sitting judges are excluded to preserve the separation of powers between the judiciary and the legislature. People who have been declared bankrupt and not yet been discharged are also disqualified, as are those who hold certain Crown offices or civil service positions that require political neutrality.

Students often mix up voting ages under exam pressure. The key distinction is that 18 applies to UK general elections and most local council elections in England, while 16 applies to Scottish Parliament elections, Senedd elections, and local elections in Scotland and Wales. In some recent local elections in England, proposals have been made to lower the age to 16, but no change had been made to general election law as of 2026. Similarly, being old enough to vote does not automatically mean you can stand for election in all contexts — some elections have separate minimum ages for candidates. Always check which election the question refers to.

What Is Voter Turnout?

Voter turnout is the percentage of registered voters who actually vote in a given election. In the 2019 UK general election, turnout was around 67 per cent. In the 2024 UK general election, turnout fell to approximately 60 per cent — one of the lower figures recorded in modern times. By contrast, turnout in the 1992 general election was around 78 per cent. These figures show that turnout varies significantly between elections.

When large numbers of eligible voters choose not to vote, this is described as voter apathy. Voter apathy is a concern for democratic health because a government elected on a very low turnout may lack a strong mandate — the democratic authority that comes from winning a clear majority of votes.

Key Fact

UK general election turnout has ranged from roughly 59% to 84% in the post-war period. The 2001 general election recorded approximately 59% — the lowest in decades — while 1992 recorded around 78%. Turnout tends to be lower in local elections and European Parliament elections than in general elections.

Why Is Voter Turnout Low? Two Viewpoints

There are different perspectives on what causes low turnout and whether it signals a crisis in democracy.

One viewpoint holds that low voter turnout reflects a genuine democratic crisis. Supporters of this position argue that when fewer people vote, the winning party represents a smaller proportion of the overall population, weakening its mandate and its claim to represent public opinion. They point to research suggesting that non-voters are disproportionately young, economically disadvantaged, or from minority communities, meaning their interests go unrepresented in Parliament.

A contrasting viewpoint suggests that low turnout does not necessarily mean citizens are disengaged from democracy as a whole. Some political scientists argue that when people do not vote, it can reflect satisfaction with the status quo rather than hostility to politics. Others point out that citizens engage politically in many other ways — through petitions, social media campaigns, pressure groups and community action — and that elections are only one channel of democratic participation.

Suggestions for Increasing Voter Turnout

A range of measures has been proposed and in some cases tested to increase participation in elections. Supporters of compulsory voting argue that making voting a legal requirement, as in Australia, ensures high participation and a stronger mandate for elected governments. Critics argue this forces people to vote without genuine engagement and may undermine the freedom not to participate — which some see as equally important to democratic freedom.

Other proposals include online voting, which supporters argue would remove barriers of travel and mobility; lowering the voting age to 16, which advocates say would build civic habits earlier; more voter education in schools; and making election day a public holiday so that working people find it easier to get to a polling station. Critics of some of these proposals argue that convenience alone does not address underlying disengagement and that quality of participation matters as much as quantity.

practice_questions.text:
What is the minimum age to vote in a UK general election?
A) 16
B) 17
C) 18
D) 21
State one group of people who are NOT allowed to vote in a UK general election.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of the following: members of the House of Lords; a person serving a custodial prison sentence; a person who is not registered to vote. One clearly stated answer is sufficient — no further explanation is required.

practice_questions.text: Explain why low voter turnout can be a problem for democracy.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. A strong answer develops a point with cause and consequence. For example: a government elected on low turnout may lack a strong mandate (1 mark) because only a small proportion of the total population voted for it (1 mark), which means it cannot claim to represent the views of most citizens (1 mark), and this weakens its democratic authority when passing laws (1 mark). Answers that state a problem without development score 1–2. Two fully developed points of cause and consequence can score up to 4.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional polling organisation surveyed 1,500 registered voters after the 2024 general election. Their report found: 'Among non-voters, the most common reasons given were disillusionment with all political parties (34%), feeling that their vote would make no difference (28%), and difficulty getting to a polling station on a working day (19%). Only 11% said they were satisfied with the result and had therefore chosen not to vote.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, what does this source suggest about ways to increase voter turnout?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying what the source shows (non-voters give disillusionment and powerlessness as the main reasons for not voting); 1 mark for interpreting the significance of this (making voting easier on a working day addresses only 19% of non-voters, so turnout measures must also tackle engagement); 1 mark for applying own knowledge (linking to proposals such as compulsory voting, online voting, or political education); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that combines the source and own knowledge (e.g. the source implies that convenience reforms alone would not solve voter apathy since disillusionment is the primary cause — deeper engagement measures are needed).

practice_questions.text:
A student council is debating whether to recommend that the local council pilot online voting for its next parish election. A local civic organisation has said: 'Making it easier to vote will automatically increase democratic participation.'

Discuss whether making voting easier is the most effective way to increase voter turnout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a sustained, balanced discussion with developed points on both sides, uses connective language, names at least one specific real-world example (e.g. Australia's compulsory voting system, the 16+ voting age in Scotland, or online voting trials in Estonia), and reaches a clear overall assessment of which measures are most effective and why.

Secure: Covers both sides with some development, includes at least one named real-world example, and reaches a general conclusion, though the reasoning may not be fully sustained.

Developing: Makes relevant points but the discussion is mainly one-sided or lacks real-world examples. May list proposals without weighing their effectiveness.

Emerging: Offers basic points about voting or turnout with little development, no named example, and no comparative judgement about the measures.

practice_questions.text:
A local charity has published a report arguing that the voting age for all UK elections should be lowered to 16, in line with the rules for Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections.

Evaluate whether lowering the voting age to 16 is the best way to increase democratic participation among young people.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full two-sided argument with multiple developed points for and against; names at least one specific real-world example per side (e.g. 16+ voting in Scottish Parliament and Senedd elections, or international examples such as Austria's national elections); reaches a substantiated overall judgement that weighs the evidence and explains why one position is stronger.

Secure: Both sides presented with at least one named real-world example; a conclusion is reached, but the evaluative judgement may lack full justification.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development; argument may be mainly one-sided or examples are generic ('in some countries') rather than named.

Emerging: Basic points about voting age with little development; one-sided or descriptive; no real-world named example; no substantiated conclusion.

Content that could be credited — Arguments in favour: Scottish Parliament and Senedd already allow 16-year-olds to vote; 16-year-olds can pay tax, marry and join the armed forces; building civic habits early may create lifelong voters; gives young people a voice on issues that affect them such as education and climate policy. Arguments against: 16-year-olds may lack life experience to make fully informed political decisions; turnout among 18-24 year olds is already lower than older age groups, so extending the age may not improve participation; other factors such as compulsory voting or better civic education may be more effective; changing the law risks party-political manipulation of which age group is more likely to support particular parties.

before.content_html:
Why Does Government Collect Tax?

Governments need money to run public services — things such as schools, hospitals, roads, the police and welfare benefits. This money is raised primarily through taxation. In the UK, central government collects most taxes, and some funding is also raised by local councils through the council tax. Without taxation, the government would be unable to provide the services that citizens rely on throughout their lives.

The UK government collects tax in several different ways. Income tax is paid by people who earn above a certain threshold — in 2024–25 the personal allowance (the amount you can earn before paying income tax) was £12,570. National Insurance is another tax on earnings that funds state benefits and the NHS. Value Added Tax (VAT) is charged at 20 per cent on most goods and services and is paid indirectly by consumers when they make purchases. Corporation tax is paid by businesses on their profits.

Key Fact

The four main forms of UK taxation are: income tax (on earnings), National Insurance (on earnings, funds benefits and the NHS), VAT (on most goods and services at 20%), and corporation tax (on company profits). Local government also raises money through council tax on residential properties.

How Is Public Money Spent?

The UK government sets out its spending plans in the annual Budget, presented to Parliament by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. The largest areas of public spending are typically health (principally the National Health Service), social protection (welfare benefits and pensions), and education. Together these three areas account for the majority of government expenditure. Other significant areas include defence, transport infrastructure, and debt interest payments on money the government has borrowed in previous years.

Local government also spends public money, funded partly by central government grants and partly by council tax. Local councils provide services including waste collection, local roads, social care for the elderly and disabled, planning, and early-years education. The budgeting process at both national and local level involves difficult trade-offs: increasing spending in one area often means cutting or holding back spending in another.

Supporters of generous welfare spending argue that a comprehensive welfare state ensures that no citizen is left without support during illness, unemployment, or old age. They contend that investment in welfare reduces poverty and inequality, generates social cohesion, and prevents the long-term costs associated with untreated mental and physical illness. They often point to the post-war settlement that created the NHS and the modern benefits system as evidence of what collective provision can achieve.

Critics of high welfare spending argue that an overly generous benefits system can reduce incentives to work and places a heavy burden on taxpayers and public debt. They suggest that welfare programmes must be means-tested and targeted at those most in need, rather than provided universally, in order to keep costs sustainable. They argue that a growing national debt creates long-term risks for the economy and future generations.

Both viewpoints reflect genuine political values about the role of the state, individual responsibility, and the balance between rights and responsibilities. There is no single “correct” answer to these debates — they form part of the ongoing democratic conversation about how public money should be used.

Health, Education and Elderly Care

The NHS provides healthcare free at the point of use to all UK residents, funded by taxation and National Insurance. It is the largest single item of day-to-day public spending. Supporters of this model argue that universal free healthcare prevents a two-tier system where only the wealthy can afford good treatment. Critics argue that the NHS faces growing demand from an ageing population and that funding pressures require either higher taxes or a different funding model.

Education is funded largely through central government grants to schools, with additional funding channelled through local authorities. Early years, primary, secondary, and further education are all publicly funded, though there is ongoing debate about how university tuition should be funded — whether primarily through student loans, general taxation, or a combination of the two.

The social care system supports elderly and disabled people who need help with daily living. Unlike the NHS, social care is not entirely free at the point of use — individuals may need to contribute to the costs of residential or home care depending on their savings. This gap between NHS funding and social care funding has been a source of significant political debate, with different parties proposing different solutions.

Key Fact

The three largest areas of UK government spending are health (the NHS), social protection (benefits and pensions), and education. Together they typically account for more than half of all public expenditure. Defence is a significant but smaller budget item.

Governments face the challenge of managing risk when making spending decisions. A sudden economic downturn, a public health emergency, or a natural disaster may require extra spending that was not planned in the annual Budget. To manage this risk, governments may hold reserves, borrow money by issuing government bonds (known as gilts), or adjust tax rates. The budget deficit occurs when spending exceeds tax revenues. When deficits accumulate over time they add to the national debt, which must eventually be repaid through future taxation or spending cuts.

Local councils face similar challenges but with much less room to manoeuvre. Unlike the central government, councils cannot borrow freely or print money. When central government grants are reduced, councils must choose which services to cut or reduce — decisions that directly affect communities and are sometimes highly controversial locally.

before.content_html:
Politics in the Digital Age

For most of British history, taking part in politics meant turning up in person — to a public meeting, a polling station or a protest march. Today, citizens can sign a petition, contact their MP, or share a campaign video without leaving their homes. Digital democracy describes how the internet and social media are reshaping the ways citizens engage with government and hold it to account.

This shift raises important questions. Does digital participation make democracy more inclusive, or does it risk concentrating political voice among those who are most connected? Understanding the advantages and limits of digital civic participation is central to evaluating how healthy British democracy is today.

E-Petitions: A Route to Parliament

One of the most widely used digital tools is the e-petition. The UK Parliament’s official petition website allows any UK resident to create or sign a petition. Once a petition reaches 10,000 signatures, the government must respond formally. If it reaches 100,000 signatures, Parliament must consider holding a debate on the issue.

Key Fact

On the UK Parliament petition website: 10,000 signatures = mandatory government response; 100,000 signatures = Parliament must consider a debate. This gives ordinary citizens a direct, low-barrier route to put an issue on the parliamentary agenda.

E-petitions have been used on a wide range of issues — from animal welfare to veterans’ housing, from road safety to climate policy. They are non-partisan: a petition calling for tougher sentences for rural crime attracts signatories from across the political spectrum, as does one calling for greater investment in mental health services. The key democratic value of the e-petition system is that it lowers the barrier to entry — a citizen does not need to be a member of a political party, know an MP personally, or have financial resources to trigger a parliamentary response.

Social Media and Political Engagement

Social media platforms have transformed how political campaigns are run and how citizens find out about public affairs. Platforms enable citizens to share news, organise events, contact politicians directly and mobilise support for causes in ways that were not possible before the internet. Online campaigning can reach millions of people at very low cost.

Supporters of digital engagement argue that it has made politics more accessible. Young people, disabled citizens and those in rural areas — groups who historically faced barriers to participation — can now engage with public affairs from home. Campaigns focused on local issues such as saving a community library or improving pedestrian crossings can mobilise residents who might never have attended a council meeting.

Critics raise several concerns about digital democracy. First, the digital divide means that elderly citizens, those in poverty and people in areas with poor internet connectivity are less likely to participate in digital forms of civic engagement. If e-petitions and online campaigns become the dominant route to political influence, the voices of these groups may be further marginalised.

Second, critics point to “slacktivism” — where signing an online petition or sharing a social media post feels like meaningful action but produces little real-world change. One viewpoint holds that digital participation can substitute for deeper civic engagement such as joining a political party, attending public meetings or volunteering. Another viewpoint is that even low-effort digital actions build political confidence and can be a gateway to more sustained participation.

Third, social media algorithms can create “filter bubbles”, where citizens mainly see content that confirms their existing views. This can make it harder to encounter different perspectives and may deepen political polarisation rather than foster the deliberate, balanced debate that democracy requires.

Other Digital Tools for Civic Participation

Beyond e-petitions and social media, citizens have access to a range of digital tools to engage with their representatives. Most MPs and local councillors maintain email addresses and social media accounts, making it easier than ever to contact them directly. Websites such as WriteToThem.com allow citizens to locate their representatives and send messages with just a postcode. Many local councils now live-stream their meetings and publish minutes online, increasing accountability and access.

Key Fact

Key digital participation tools include: e-petitions (Parliament website), direct contact with MPs by email or social media, online council meeting access, and crowdfunding platforms for community campaigns. Each provides a different route for citizens to make their voice heard without traditional face-to-face engagement.

Voting and Digital Technology

Some commentators and politicians have proposed extending digital technology to the act of voting itself, through e-voting. Supporters argue it could increase voter turnout by making voting more convenient, especially for young voters, shift workers, and people with mobility difficulties.

Critics warn that e-voting raises serious concerns about cybersecurity, the risk of electoral fraud and the potential loss of the secret ballot. The UK Electoral Commission has conducted trials of online voting in local elections, but no national e-voting system has been introduced. The debate continues, with one viewpoint emphasising the need to modernise democracy and another stressing the importance of proven, secure systems that citizens can trust.

A common error in exam answers is to treat all digital actions as equally meaningful forms of political participation. Examiners reward candidates who can distinguish between depth of participation. Signing an e-petition takes seconds and may or may not lead to change; joining a formal citizens’ assembly, attending a council scrutiny meeting or sustained volunteering represents much deeper engagement. When you are asked to “evaluate” digital democracy, always weigh the benefits of wider reach against the risk that shallow online actions replace deeper civic involvement.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the threshold for a UK e-petition to trigger a parliamentary debate?
A) 1,000 signatures
B) 10,000 signatures
C) 50,000 signatures
D) 100,000 signatures
State what is meant by the term 'digital divide' in the context of political participation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that not all citizens have equal access to digital technology or the internet; 1 mark for developing this by linking it to political participation (e.g. those without internet access are less able to participate in e-petitions, online campaigns or digital contact with MPs, creating unequal political voice).

practice_questions.text: Explain how e-petitions allow citizens to contribute to parliamentary democracy and hold those in power to account.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying that citizens can create or sign petitions online on the UK Parliament website; 1 mark for explaining the 10,000-signature threshold that triggers a mandatory government response; 1 mark for explaining the 100,000-signature threshold that triggers a potential parliamentary debate; 1 mark for a developed explanation linking this to accountability (e.g. government must respond formally to public concern, creating a mechanism to challenge or influence policy without needing party membership or financial resources).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional newspaper article published in 2024 reported: 'A petition calling for the introduction of free school breakfast clubs in all state primary schools gathered 127,000 signatures within three weeks of being posted on the Parliament petition website. The government's response, published six weeks later, stated it was "keeping the matter under review". Campaign organisers said the formal government response showed the petition system was working; critics argued that a non-committal government answer was not meaningful accountability.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, assess what this source tells us about the effectiveness of e-petitions as a tool for holding government to account.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant point from the source (e.g. the petition reached over 100,000 signatures, triggering a formal government response); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. the threshold system does create a formal accountability mechanism, placing the issue on the government's agenda); 1 mark for a limitation or counter-point drawn from the source or own knowledge (e.g. a non-committal response suggests the government is not obliged to act, limiting the petition's impact beyond publicity); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining the source with own knowledge (e.g. e-petitions are more effective at generating a public record of concern than at forcing policy change, which typically requires sustained campaigning beyond the petition stage).

practice_questions.text:
A local youth council is debating whether the rise of social media and online campaigning has made British democracy more or less effective. One member argues that digital tools have transformed participation for the better; another argues they have created new problems without solving old ones.

Discuss the view that digital democracy has improved political participation in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Presents a well-developed two-sided argument with specific examples on each side (e.g. e-petition thresholds, the digital divide, filter bubbles, increased MP accessibility via email). Uses connectives to weigh opposing viewpoints and reaches a substantiated judgement about overall impact. Named institutions or mechanisms (Parliament petition website, Electoral Commission e-voting trials) anchor the argument.

Secure: Covers both sides of the argument with at least one developed point per side and one named example. Generally accurate. Argument is two-sided in places but may not fully weigh the evidence.

Developing: Identifies relevant advantages and disadvantages but develops them unevenly, or the argument is largely one-sided. Some reference to real-world examples but limited depth.

Emerging: Lists basic points for or against digital participation. Little or no real-world example. Descriptive rather than analytical.

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the claim that digital democracy has made political participation in the UK more equal and effective.

In your answer you should consider arguments in support of this claim, arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Digital tools lower participation barriers (e.g. e-petitions require only internet access, not party membership or wealth); Parliament e-petition website creates a formal accountability route (10,000 = government response, 100,000 = debate); social media enables citizens in rural areas, disabled people, and young voters to engage without attending physical events; direct MP contact by email is easier than writing letters; increased transparency through live-streamed council meetings.

Arguments against: The digital divide (elderly, low-income, rural communities with poor connectivity) means digital participation may increase inequality rather than reduce it; slacktivism risk — shallow online actions may substitute for deeper civic involvement; filter bubbles reduce exposure to opposing viewpoints, harming deliberative democracy; security concerns and potential for misinformation in e-voting proposals; government responses to e-petitions are non-binding, limiting real accountability.

Mastering: Sustained two-sided evaluation with named examples on each side, clear weighing of evidence, and a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond 'it depends' (e.g. digital democracy has improved reach but not depth of participation, and structural inequalities must be addressed before claiming it is truly more equal).

Secure: Both sides covered with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but it may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development, one-sided, or conclusion is a summary rather than an evaluation.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive rather than evaluative.

glossary_terms.definition: The use of digital technologies such as the internet, social media and e-petition platforms to increase citizen participation in democratic processes.
An online petition hosted on an official government or Parliament website, which can trigger a parliamentary debate if it reaches the required number of signatures.
The use of social media platforms to organise, publicise or support a campaign or cause, often aiming to drive signatures, donations or attendance.
The gap between those who have access to digital technology and the internet and those who do not, which can create inequalities in political participation.
The obligation of those in power to explain and justify their decisions to the public and to face consequences if they act improperly.
A system that would allow citizens to cast their vote in an election via the internet or a secure digital device, rather than attending a polling station.
The proportion of eligible voters who actually cast a vote in an election.

lessons.title: Citizens in Action: Two Case Studies

before.content_html:
Why Case Studies Matter

The specification asks you to know two contrasting examples of how citizens working together have attempted to change or improve their communities. These examples should demonstrate different methods and different contexts, so that you can compare and evaluate how citizens use collective action to address public policy, challenge injustice or resolve a community issue. Citizenship action can be local, national or international, and can focus on issues from across the political spectrum.

This lesson examines two case studies: first, the Hillsborough families’ campaign for justice; second, the campaign by disability rights organisations that contributed to the Equality Act 2010. Both are factual accounts of civic action and its outcomes, presented as models of how citizens can make a difference through sustained, organised effort.

Case Study 1: The Hillsborough Families’ Campaign

On 15 April 1989, ninety-seven people died in a crush at Hillsborough football stadium in Sheffield during an FA Cup semi-final. (A ninety-eighth victim died in 2021.) The initial official narrative wrongly blamed supporters for the disaster. Families of those who died refused to accept this account and began a campaign for the truth and legal accountability.

The Hillsborough Family Support Group used a wide range of methods over more than three decades. They petitioned Parliament, gathered and preserved evidence, engaged solicitors and barristers, lobbied MPs and successive governments, and worked with journalists to keep the issue in the public eye. In 2012, the Hillsborough Independent Panel published a report showing that 96 victims were unlawfully killed and that there had been a cover-up by South Yorkshire Police and others.

Key Fact

The Hillsborough families used petitions, legal action, lobbying, media engagement and sustained public campaigning over more than 30 years. Key outcomes: the 2012 Independent Panel report confirmed unlawful killing; in 2016 the original inquest verdicts were quashed and a new inquest jury returned unlawful killing verdicts for 96 of the 97 victims.

The Hillsborough case illustrates several important citizenship principles. First, that ordinary citizens without formal political power can challenge state institutions and achieve justice through sustained, evidence-based campaigning. Second, that legal processes (inquests, judicial review, criminal investigation) are an important route alongside political pressure. Third, that the campaign required decades of perseverance and that meaningful change in complex cases takes time.

Case Study 2: Disability Rights and the Equality Act 2010

The Equality Act 2010 is a landmark piece of legislation that consolidated and strengthened protections against discrimination in the UK. It brought together previous laws on sex, race and disability discrimination and extended protection to nine protected characteristics. Its passage was shaped by decades of campaigning by disability rights organisations, women’s groups and equality bodies.

Disability rights organisations such as Scope and the Disability Rights Commission campaigned throughout the 1990s and 2000s for stronger legal protections. Their methods included direct advocacy to MPs and ministers, evidence submissions to parliamentary committees, public awareness campaigns, and legal challenges under existing equality legislation to test and extend its boundaries. The Disability Discrimination Act 1995 was an early result; the Equality Act 2010 consolidated and strengthened those rights further.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 covers nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. It applies to employment, education, housing and the provision of services.

This case study illustrates a different model of citizenship action. Rather than responding to a single injustice (as the Hillsborough families did), disability rights organisations pursued a long-term legislative strategy across multiple parliaments and governments. They combined insider tactics (formal consultations, committee evidence, working with sympathetic MPs) with outsider tactics (public campaigns and demonstrations), demonstrating that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive.

The Hillsborough and disability rights campaigns differ in several important ways. The Hillsborough campaign focused on a single specific injustice and pursued legal justice through the courts and inquests alongside political lobbying. The disability rights campaign pursued systemic legislative change across a wider range of issues and over a longer strategic timeline.

Both campaigns, however, share important features: they involved citizens working collectively rather than individually; they combined multiple methods (legal, political, media, public); they required persistence over years or decades; and they achieved tangible, lasting changes (the 2016 inquest verdicts; the Equality Act 2010). Both demonstrate that citizens can achieve meaningful outcomes even against powerful institutions, provided they are organised, evidence-based and persistent.

Evaluating Citizenship Actions

When you are asked to evaluate a citizenship action in the exam, you need to assess both process and outcome. Did the action achieve its stated aim? If not fully, did it make progress? Were the methods used appropriate and effective? What were the limitations or unintended consequences? A strong evaluation will consider impact from multiple perspectives — the citizens who took action, those the action was meant to help, and the wider democratic system.

Students often evaluate citizenship actions in binary terms — either “it worked” or “it failed”. Exam mark schemes reward more nuanced thinking. A campaign can partially succeed: it may change public awareness without changing law; it may change law without changing behaviour; it may achieve its immediate aim but reveal deeper structural problems. Strong evaluative answers assess what was achieved, what was not, and why — considering factors such as the resources available to the campaign, the political climate at the time, and whether the methods chosen matched the aims.

practice_questions.text:
The Equality Act 2010 protects citizens from discrimination on the basis of a number of 'protected characteristics'. Which of the following is NOT a protected characteristic under the Act?
A) Disability
B) Nationality of birth country
C) Religion or belief
D) Age
practice_questions.marks: B) Nationality of birth country [1 mark]. Note: Race (which includes nationality and ethnic origin) is a protected characteristic, but 'nationality of birth country' as a standalone category is not a precise protected characteristic listed in the Act. Examiners would credit responses demonstrating knowledge that race is protected while distinguishing the specific phrasing.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'citizenship action'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that citizenship action involves citizens taking planned steps to bring about a change in policy, law or public life; 1 mark for developing this by noting that it can be carried out by individuals or groups and may target local, national or international issues.

practice_questions.text: Describe two methods used by citizens working through groups to challenge injustice, using examples from the case studies you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per method). Method 1: legal challenges through courts and inquests — for example, the Hillsborough families pursued new inquest proceedings that in 2016 returned unlawful killing verdicts, using the legal system alongside political campaigning (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed or linked to a named example). Method 2: direct advocacy to MPs, ministers and parliamentary committees — for example, disability rights organisations including Scope submitted evidence to select committees, influencing the development of the Equality Act 2010 (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below.

A fictional newspaper analysis piece from 2025 stated: 'Research tracking 40 citizen campaigns over a 20-year period found that campaigns combining legal action with sustained public advocacy were three times more likely to achieve their stated aims than those relying on a single method alone. The study also found that campaigns with a specific, focused aim outperformed those with broad or vague goals.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, assess what this source tells us about what makes a citizenship action effective.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant point from the source (e.g. using multiple methods increases the likelihood of success); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. campaigns that combine legal, political and public routes are more powerful than single-method ones); 1 mark for supporting this with own knowledge (e.g. the Hillsborough campaign combined legal processes and public lobbying; disability rights groups combined insider advocacy and public campaigns); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. focus and persistence are also important factors, as demonstrated by campaigns that maintained a clear objective over many years).

practice_questions.text:
A community group is planning a campaign to improve facilities for young people in a local park that has been neglected. The group is debating whether to focus on direct action and public pressure or to work through formal channels such as council meetings and petitions.

Discuss the view that working through formal channels is the most effective way for citizens to bring about change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Well-developed two-sided discussion with specific named examples on each side (e.g. Hillsborough families using formal legal processes; disability rights groups using formal committee evidence, but also both using public campaigns). Uses connectives to weigh evidence and reaches a substantiated judgement about when formal channels are most or least effective.

Secure: Both sides covered with at least one developed point per side and one named example. Two-sided in places; generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but develops unevenly; largely one-sided or without named examples.

Emerging: Basic points, little or no named example, descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the view that collective citizenship action — citizens working through groups — is a more effective way to bring about change than individual citizens acting alone.

In your answer, consider arguments in support of this view, arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: collective action provides greater resources, expertise and public profile than individuals can achieve alone; groups can sustain campaigns over time better than individuals; named examples show the power of collective action (Hillsborough Family Support Group over 30 years; disability rights organisations across multiple parliaments); groups can combine insider and outsider tactics simultaneously; collective campaigns attract media attention more effectively; they give marginalised communities a larger voice.

Arguments against: individual citizens can sometimes act faster and more flexibly than organisations; individual whistleblowers and campaigners (e.g. individuals who gathered and published evidence on corporate or state wrongdoing) can trigger change; groups can be divided or captured by internal politics; organised groups can represent narrow interests and may not speak for the communities they claim to represent.

Mastering: Sustained two-sided evaluation with named examples on both sides; weighs evidence; substantiated conclusion (e.g. collective action is generally more effective for sustained change against powerful institutions, but individuals can play a crucial catalytic role, particularly in triggering initial public awareness).

Secure: Both sides with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development, or one-sided, or conclusion is a summary.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive.
